newsitem.title: INDIA: Sparring India groups under pressure to avert poll.
newsitem.headline: Sparring India groups under pressure to avert poll.

text.p: Leaders of India's defeated coalition and its lost ally, the Congress party, wrangled over the possibility of setting up a new government and averting snap elections.

There were signs that the United Front alliance would agree to replace its leader, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, in a last-ditch effort to prevent elections. But officially, neither group conceded ground to the other.

Deve Gowda, whose centre-left alliance was defeated in a vote of confidence on Friday, indicated that he was ready for fresh elections but few lawmakers wanted to face voters only a year after the last polls.
Partners in the 15-party alliance criticised Deve Gowda's stance, saying they were in no mood for a mid-term poll, a close aide of a key negotiator told Reuters.

As a final resort, the United Front, whose decision-making Steering Committee was due to meet at 7 p.m. (1330 GMT), might have to accept the Congress demand and replace its leader, he said. "There is no other way," he said.

The United Front govenrment was set up last June under an agreement with Congress to oust a 12-day-old administration formed by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), accused by both of bias against India's minority Moslems.

On March 30, Congress president Sitaram Kesri withdrew its vital support to the minority alliance, which has only 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house, Lok Sabha, saying it had failed to contain the BJP.

The decision by Congress, which has 140 members, meant that Deve Gowda lost Friday's confidence vote. Congress has since set only one condition -- his resignation -- for its renewed support but the United Front has steadfastly refused this.
But hardliners in both the United Front and Congress faced dissent in their own ranks from deputies who said they were not ready for elections.
Some of Deve Gowda's allies did not share his optimism that his 10-month performance in government was good enough to ensure electoral success in a snap poll.

Kesri faced a near-revolt when 100 Congress deputies met at the house of senior leader Sharad Pawar, seething that they were forced to vote against their wishes on Friday and pushed to the verge of elections they wished to avoid.
"They were all very angry. They said how long can we go on suffering like this?" a Congress lawmaker told Reuters.
